title: Response to application from respondent Richard Comerford, Secretary, Florida Department of Corrections

pages.text:
No. 26A415
CAPITAL CASE
EXECUTION SCHEDULED FOR
TUESDAY, SEPT. 29, 2026, AT 6:00 P.M.
IN THE
SUPREME COURT OF THE UNITED STATES
CURTIS W. BEASLEY,
Petitioner,
v.
RICHARD COMERFORD,
SECRETARY, FLORIDA DEPARTMENT OF CORRECTIONS,
Respondent.
ON PETITION FOR A WRIT OF CERTIORARI
TO THE UNITED STATES COURT OF APPEALS
FOR THE ELEVENTH CIRCUIT
RESPONSE TO APPLICATION FOR STAY OF EXECUTION
On September 24, 2026, Petitioner, Curtis Wilkie Beasley, represented by 
state postconviction counsel Bjorn E. Brunvand and J. Jervis Wise of the law firm of 
Brunvand, Wise, & Farinella, filed, in this Court, a petition for writ of certiorari 
seeking review of a decision by the Eleventh Circuit Court of Appeals in this active 
warrant case. The petition seeks review of an unpublished decision by the Eleventh 
Circuit denying his motion for a certificate of appealability (COA) from the district 
court’s denial of a Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 60(b) motion seeking to vacate its 
2010 judgment denying Beasley’s federal habeas petition. Beasley has also filed an

2
application for a stay of execution based on the petition for certiorari. This Court, 
however, should simply deny the petition and then deny the stay.
Stays of Execution
Stays of executions are not granted as “a matter of course.” Hill v. McDonough, 
547 U.S. 573, 583-84 (2006). Rather, a stay of execution is “an equitable remedy” and 
“equity must be sensitive to the State’s strong interest in enforcing its criminal 
judgments without undue interference from the federal courts.” Id. at 584. There is a 
“strong equitable presumption against the grant of a stay where a claim could have 
been brought at such a time as to allow consideration of the merits without requiring 
entry of a stay.” Nelson v. Campbell, 541 U.S. 637, 650 (2004). Equity must also 
consider “an inmate’s attempt at manipulation.” Gomez v. U.S. Dist. Ct. for N. Dist. 
of Cal., 503 U.S. 653, 654 (1992). “Both the State and the victims of crime have an 
important interest in the timely enforcement of a sentence.” Calderon v. Thompson, 
523 U.S. 538, 556 (1998). This Court has highlighted the State’s and the victims’
interests in the timely enforcement of the death sentence. Bucklew v. Precythe, 587 
U.S. 119, 149-151 (2019). The people of Florida, as well as the families of the victims 
of capital crimes, deserve better than the excessive delays that now typically occur in 
capital cases. Id. at 149. The Court has stated that courts should police carefully 
against last-minute claims being used “as tools to interpose unjustified delay” in 
executions. Id. at 150. This Court has also repeatedly stated that last-minute stays 
of execution should be the “extreme exception, not the norm.” Barr v. Lee, 591 U.S.

3
979, 981 (2020) (quoting Bucklew, 587 U.S. at 151, and vacating a lower court’s grant 
of a stay of a federal execution).
To be granted a stay of execution in this Court, Beasley must establish three 
factors: (1) a reasonable probability that the Court would vote to grant certiorari; (2) 
a significant possibility of reversal if review was granted; and (3) a likelihood of 
irreparable injury to the applicant in the absence of a stay. Barefoot v. Estelle, 463 
U.S. 880, 895 (1983). He must establish all three factors.
Probability of This Court Granting Certiorari Review
As to the first factor, there is little chance that four justices of this Court would 
vote to grant certiorari review on the issues raised in Beasley’s petition. The Eleventh 
Circuit’s two-paragraph unpublished decision does not conflict with any decision by 
this Court or a United States court of appeals, nor does it decide any important and 
unsettled question of federal law. See Sup. Ct. R. 10(a), (c). The order merely states 
that Beasley had not made a substantial showing of the denial of a constitutional
right as required to warrant a COA under 28 U.S.C. § 2253(c). The order did not 
discuss the district court’s findings that Beasley challenges in his petition, to wit, 
whether the Rule 60(b) motion was time-barred and whether it stated a cognizable 
basis for federal habeas relief. And even if the Eleventh Circuit’s order could be 
construed as an endorsement of the district court’s reasoning, it is unpublished and, 
therefore, does not constitute binding precedent. There is little probability that the 
Court would vote to grant review under these circumstances. Beasley fails the first 
factor, which alone is sufficient to deny the motion for a stay.

4
Significant Possibility of Reversal
As to the second factor, there is not a significant possibility of reversal on the 
issues raised by Beasley. First, as the Eleventh Circuit indicated, the Rule 60(b) 
motion was subject to dismissal as an unauthorized second or successive federal 
habeas petition. See Fernandez v. United States, 146 S. Ct. 1292, 1301 (2026); Rivers 
v. Guerrero, 605 U.S. 443, 453 (2025). Second, the motion was also time-barred 
because it was premised on newly discovered evidence, it was filed outside the oneyear time limit for motions based on such evidence under Rule 60(b)(2), and Beasley 
could not use Rule 60(b)(6) to circumvent the time bar. See Kemp v. United States, 
596 U.S. 528, 531-39 (2022). Third, Beasley would not be entitled to relief under Rule 
60(b)(6) regardless, because Beasley does not qualify for any exemption from 
execution under this Court’s precedent. Ultimately, there was no error at all in the 
proceedings below, let alone one that warrants certiorari review.
Irreparable Injury
As to the third factor of irreparable injury, none is identified. While the 
execution will result in Beasley’s death, that is the inherent nature of a death 
sentence. The stay standard, derived from ordinary civil litigation, does not naturally 
fit the capital context, where finality is the execution itself. Beasley identifies no 
harm beyond that consequence. Moreover, this Court has stated in the capital context 
that “the relative harms to the parties” must still be considered, including “the State’s 
significant interest in enforcing its criminal judgments.” Nelson, 541 U.S. at 649-50 
(emphasis added). Without finality, “the criminal law is deprived of much of its

5
deterrent effect.” Calderon, 523 U.S. at 555-56. The murder of Carolyn Monfort for 
which Beasley was sentenced to death occurred in 1995, and his death sentence has 
been final since 2001. Beasley fails this factor as well.
Equity Does Not Warrant a Stay
Finally, equity does not warrant a stay. Again, a stay of execution is an 
extraordinary equitable remedy, and this Court has emphasized that last-minute 
stays should be the “extreme exception, not the norm.” Lee, 591 U.S. at 981. Beasley 
has had decades to challenge his death sentence, and all of his collateral challenges 
have failed. He should not be granted additional time merely to attempt to raise 
further meritless challenges to his long-final death sentence. Moreover, the 
underlying premise of Beasley’s new claim is that the State has waited longer than it 
should have to execute him. That weighs against, not in favor of, a stay of execution. 
As well, the State’s compelling interest in the timely enforcement of its criminal 
judgments and the corresponding interest in finality for the victim’s family weigh 
decisively against a stay. The application should be denied.

6
